title: The Wooden Lighthouse
body: From early 1873 a timber lighthouse stood just seaward of where Queen Street meets Marine Terrace, guiding ships in to the jetty. Local carpenter Charles Keyser built it from timber supplied by the Lockeville-Ballarat Timber Company at Wonnerup. It stood 70 feet high, its kerosene lamp could be seen from 21 miles away, and a ship's bell hanging from its beams was rung whenever a ship arrived. Once the jetty reached its full length a small beacon at the far end took over, and demolition began on 7 April 1933.

place.name: Foreshore at the north end of Queen Street

sticker: A tall skinny timber lighthouse with a glowing lamp on top and a little brass bell swinging from its beams

title: Justice by the Jetty
body: The Old Courthouse complex was put here in 1860 because it was handy to the jetty. A courtroom and bond store came first, and in 1861 a police office, gaol cells, stables, a fodder room, police cottages and a magistrate's retiring room were added. Rooms for the post and telegraph followed in 1873, a new court house in 1897, and the custom house was once linked to the jetty by a tramway. The police moved out in 1976, the Busselton Arts Council moved in, and the new arts complex opened in 1985.

place.name: Old Courthouse complex, Queen Street at Marine Terrace

sticker: A little whitewashed gaol cell with a cheerful paintbrush poking out between the window bars

title: Named for the Saltwater People
body: The City of Busselton says its new arts and convention centre on Queen Street, Saltwater, is named after the Wadandi, the Saltwater People, who are the Traditional Owners of this Country, Undalup. Council endorsed the name in 2022 after community consultation and advice from the Saltwater Aboriginal Advisory Panel. Planning went back to a 2004 cultural mapping report, and the venue officially opened in May 2026. Built into it is Noongar artist Sandra Hill's work Gulyarra Gabbi Djalum Kalleep, which the City translates as The Meeting Place of the Saltwater Camp.

place.name: Saltwater Busselton, Queen Street

sticker: A gentle blue wave curling over a ring of campfire stones on golden sand

title: Before the Library Came
body: Weld Hall, on the corner of Queen and Adelaide streets, went up between 1874 and 1881 as a Mechanics' Institute, the kind of place that offered learning and support before public libraries were formalised. It was named after Frederick Aloysius Weld, Governor of Western Australia from 1869 to 1875. Since then it has been a town hall, an RSL meeting place, a rehearsal hall for the district band and even a stand-in classroom. The Repertory Club has used it since 1960, and in 2023 work began to fold it into the new performing arts centre next door.

place.name: Weld Hall, corner of Queen and Adelaide streets

sticker: A small old hall with a stack of books on its steps and a pair of theatre masks peeking out the door

title: Look Up for the Vasse
body: There has been a hotel called the Vasse on this corner since at least 1888. An 1896 advertisement offered six sitting rooms and nine bedrooms, and the building on the corner of Queen and Duchess streets dates from 1906. Large sections of it were knocked down for the shopping centre works of 2002 and 2003, but the parapet survived. Look up and you can still read the words Vasse Hotel standing out in raised lettering.

place.name: Corner of Queen and Duchess streets

sticker: A fancy old parapet with curly scrolls and a tiny frothy beer glass balanced on top

title: Holidays for the Goldfields
body: The Esplanade Hotel on Marine Terrace was designed to meet the needs of summer visitors from the goldfields. Busselton architect H. Cowell Ashton drew it up, and when the first builder withdrew with money troubles, contractor Robert Donald finished the job. It held an opening event in July 1900, with 45 rooms and space for 60 boarders. In 1952 it was bought by William Gray, who had moved down from the wheatbelt town of Narambeen to live closer to the ocean.

place.name: Marine Terrace, outside the old Esplanade Hotel site

sticker: A dusty gold miner in a sunhat dipping his toes in the sea, his pickaxe resting on a striped beach towel

title: Family Reunions Only
body: A burial ground was already marked on Busselton's 1839 town plan, and it was formally declared a cemetery in 1856. The oldest grave identified is Henry John Yelverton's, from 1854, though he probably wasn't the first. By 1900 worries about the water table meant burials were limited to what were called reunions, in graves where family already lay. Burials had stopped by the early 1930s after more than 250, and in 1961 a plan to abandon the cemetery was defeated at a public meeting.

place.name: Pioneer Cemetery, Stanley Street

sticker: A cosy little headstone with a sprig of wildflowers and a family of tiny birds lined up along its top

title: Two Dollars a Relic
body: On 4 April 1978 Cyclone Alby brought winds of up to 175 km/h and a 1.1 metre storm surge. Four sections of the promenade jetty broke away and wedged under the skeleton jetty, which survived, held in place by the weight of its railway line. No ships had used the jetty since 1972 and the State decided to remove it, so locals formed a Save the Jetty committee and sold polished jarrah blocks from the wreckage for $2 each, stamped BUSSELTON JETTY RELIC.

place.name: Foreshore beside the jetty entrance

sticker: A shiny polished block of jarrah wood with a little gold crown and pine tree stamped on top

title: The Whale That Wasn't Built
body: The favourite design for a new Australian Underwater Discovery Centre at the jetty was The Cetacean, shaped as a homage to the whales that migrate along Geographe Bay. The federal government pledged $13 million in 2019. Then, about a month before construction was due to start, the contractor revealed the project was roughly $25 million over budget, with materials up 63 per cent and shipping up 280 per cent. In May 2022 the observatory was put on the back burner until the money could be found.

place.name: Busselton foreshore, east of the jetty

sticker: A chubby whale-shaped building with round porthole windows, half under a curling wave

title: From Forty-Nine Finishers
body: The Busselton Festival of Triathlon started a long way from here, in Midland in 1983, when just 49 people finished the first race. It moved to Rottnest, spent 1988 in Collie after severe weather disrupted the 1987 Rottnest race, tried Margaret River in 2001 and outgrew it within a year, then settled in Busselton in 2002. From 2010 it was part of the Ironman 70.3 series. In 2025 it drew 2,320 competitors and an estimated 5,800 spectators over two days.

place.name: Busselton foreshore near Barnard Park

sticker: A puffed but happy triathlete in goggles and a swim cap, running with a towel flapping behind like a cape

title: The Church Meant for Augusta
body: The money for this church was first raised for a church and parsonage at Augusta, £280 in all, and £20 of it came from Queen Adelaide. But Augusta was almost deserted by then, so the Bussells advised building near the Vasse River instead. Frances Bussell laid the foundation stone on 4 March 1844, settlers quarried the stone and carted the timber, and the whole job cost £300. St Mary's opened on 11 April 1845 with its inside unfinished and a floor of beaten earth.

place.name: St Mary's Church, corner of Queen Street and Peel Terrace

sticker: A little limestone church with a tiny golden crown perched on its roof and a pair of muddy boots by the door

title: The Rector's Paddle Steamer
body: In 1939 the rector of St Mary's, Canon Robert Davies, built a miniature paddle steamer called the Jumna. It could carry up to three people. The Jumna made its first trip in early 1940 and its last on 20 April 1963, more than 23 years later. It has since been restored, and you can see it in a weatherproof cage at the Old Butter Factory museum, a short walk east along Peel Terrace from his church.

place.name: Arthur and Norah Breeden Park, on the Vasse River

sticker: A tiny red paddle steamer with a spinning wheel and a puff of smoke, carrying three cheerful passengers

title: Butter by the River
body: The Old Butter Factory on Peel Terrace was designed by the Public Works Department under chief architect Hillson Beasley, and T.J. Green won the 1917 contract with a tender of £1,751 10s 6d. The State Government opened it in 1918 to replace an earlier dairy in the Fairlawn district, which the heritage record calls the first butter factory in Western Australia. Butter making stopped in 1951, and the building opened as a museum in 1975. A fire in 2018 badly damaged the upper floor and destroyed many collection items.

place.name: Old Butter Factory museum, Peel Terrace

sticker: A golden pat of butter with a little dairy cow peeking over it beside a red brick factory

title: The Rotunda Came Ashore
body: In 1898 a pavilion was built out at the No. 1 head of the jetty, the end of the 1875 jetty, and locals knew it as the Rotunda. It hosted band performances until it was pulled down in 1958. In 1995 Bob Walker built a replica from old photographs, using recycled jetty timbers and $6,000 from the South West Development Commission. Instead of going back over the water, it now stands on the bank of the Vasse River in the Old Butter Factory precinct.

place.name: Riverbank behind the Old Butter Factory

sticker: A little round bandstand with a pointy roof and a trumpet resting on its railing beside a river

title: Bagging Up the River Mud
body: For decades nutrient-rich sediment built up on the bed of the Lower Vasse River, helping fuel its summer algal blooms. Over about seven weeks to May 2022, some 630 tonnes of dry sediment was dredged out between the Causeway Road bridge and a point upstream of the Peel Terrace footbridge. The slurry was pumped into porous geotextile bags so the water could drain back into the river, then dried for another six months before being used as daily cover at the Dunsborough landfill.

place.name: Rotary Park, on the Vasse River

sticker: A big lumpy sandbag full of river mud with a relieved little fish swimming in clear water beside it

title: A Sister Town Near Tokyo
body: Busselton has had a sister city relationship with Sugito in Japan since 1996, and it was renewed in 2016 for another 20 years. Sugito, about 40 minutes north of Tokyo by train, gave the town a Japanese garden beside the library. A Japanese elm planted in 1997 to mark the friendship grows in the gardens of the City's administration building, and a colourful mural of Sugito's mascot, Sugipyon, was painted on the Busselton Boulevard shopping centre in Prince Street for the 20th anniversary.

place.name: City of Busselton administration building, Southern Drive

sticker: A little Japanese elm tree with a red paper lantern hanging from one branch

title: Haifordshire's Grim Start
body: The odd name on Haifordshire Loop goes back to John Hurford, who called his land, Sussex Location 6, Haifordshire. He was granted 1,000 acres here in the 1840s. In 1855 he was murdered in a notorious case, and his wife Bridget, formerly Larkin, was hanged that October as an accessory, the first woman executed in Western Australia. After that the land sat largely undeveloped for years, until it was offered for sale as Broadwater Farm by 1882.

place.name: Haifordshire Fields

sticker: A lonely wooden farm gate standing in a field of long golden grass with a crow perched on top

title: A Family in the Kitchen
body: Landgate's naming record for Broadwater says Alfred Pickmore Bussell built, or had built, the first part of the Broadwater homestead, and lived there with his wife Ellen and their first three children. That first family home is what's now the old kitchen section of the homestead, and it has been restored. The little park here was formally named Homestead Park in 2004, after the old Broadwater homestead nearby.

place.name: Homestead Park

sticker: A tiny cottage kitchen with a smoking chimney and three little pairs of gumboots lined up by the door

title: The River Once Called Dalton
body: The stream beside this park is the New River, and Landgate's record suggests it got that name because settlers didn't know it was there until Frederick Ludlow crossed it in June 1834. John Molloy wrote of the New River in February 1835, but noted he had first called it the Dalton. It runs about 5.5 kilometres east from The Broadwater to join the Vasse River, and a 2008 DEC overview names it as one of the main waterbird breeding areas in the Busselton wetlands.

place.name: New River Park

sticker: A shy little river winding through the reeds with a black swan sitting on a nest in the rushes

title: The Mason's Farmhouse
body: The limestone cottage on the corner of Seymour and Abbey streets dates from about 1865. It's believed to have been built by Christopher Weetman, an English mason and master bricklayer who also supervised the volunteer labour on St Joseph's Catholic Church in Kent Street. He lived here with his wife and two daughters until he died in 1867. In 1870 his daughter Ellen married John Abbey, who took over the property, then described as one mile from the Busselton Post Office.

place.name: Corner of Seymour and Abbey streets

sticker: A squat little limestone cottage with a trowel and a neat stack of bricks leaning by the front door

title: Land Left for Learning
body: Busselton Senior High School stands on land that came from the Sayers family. The City's heritage listing says Carinia Sayers, a Wardandi Noongar man from the Vasse region, lived at Cattle Chosen with the Bussell family and married Flora in 1891, and Flora is remembered as one of the district's pioneer women. Both wished their land to become a site for education. It was never written down, but after Flora died in 1955 their children transferred it to the Education Department, and the school opened in 1958.

place.name: Busselton Senior High School, Bussell Highway frontage

sticker: A school satchel resting under a big shady peppermint tree with a pencil tucked into its strap

title: The River Sent to Sea
body: This channel was built in 1927 to cut the risk of floods in Busselton. It diverts around 90 per cent of the upper Vasse River and 60 per cent of the Sabina River straight out to Geographe Bay. Busselton still flooded in 1963, 1964, 1965, 1986, 1997 and 1999, so the 6.3 kilometre drain was upgraded to handle a one-in-100-year storm, finishing in winter 2021 with more than 130,000 seedlings planted along the way.

place.name: Vasse Diversion Drain bridge

sticker: A straight blue canal with a little fish holding up a fin to point the way to the sea

title: The Gulch on Kent Street
body: This house on Kent Street was built from 1856 as a customs house and bond store. It was later used as police quarters, and today it's a private home, so admire it from the street. Over the years it has also been known as the Resident Magistrate's Office, the Police Residence and, for reasons its heritage record never explains, The Gulch. It was added to the State Register of Heritage Places on 8 January 2010.

place.name: Kent Street, outside The Gulch

sticker: A sturdy little stone storehouse with a big iron padlock and a wooden barrel by the door

title: Missed His Own Opening
body: The Sussex Masonic Lodge on West Street opened in March 1934 as the first Masonic temple built in the Sussex district. It was designed by architect George Temple Poole, who died just before the opening ceremony, and built by local builder Robert Donald. The outside has barely changed, apart from render and paint added between 2008 and 2015. Look for the square and compass in raised relief above the porch, and a Star of David at the centre of the rose window on the eastern side.

place.name: West Street, outside the Sussex Masonic Lodge

sticker: A tiny classical hall with a big round rose window glowing like a stained-glass sun

title: The Thousand Pound Office
body: The Sussex Road Board ran the district outside the Busselton townsite, and for years it rented the town's council chambers for its monthly meetings at £20 a year. When it decided to build its own offices, ratepayers protested the £1,000 cost in October 1935, but the motion to go ahead was carried. Vice-chairman John Henry Atkinson, a building contractor, drew the plan, R. Donald and Son built it in 1936, and since the 1970s it has been a community hall.

place.name: High Street, beside the old Sussex Road Board office

sticker: A neat little cream office building with a fat money bag sitting on its front step

title: Bread And Washday
body: Wonnerup House had a busy little work building alongside the main home. Its scullery, dairy, cellar and kitchen were grouped together, and the heritage record lists a bread oven, wooden wash tubs and a cheese press in the scullery. The main house was built from limestone and pit-hewn timber, while Jim Layman later added limestone stables. The surviving rooms record the everyday work of running this farm.

place.name: Layman Road verge outside Wonnerup House

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a wooden wash tub beside a bread oven and a little cheese press, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Land For Lessons
body: In 1873 George Layman II handed over land to the colonial government in exchange for a school building. The little schoolroom went up that year, and the Heritage Council's assessment dates the separate teacher's house to 1884. The heritage record describes a single classroom and a two-room home for the teacher, across the road from Wonnerup House. A local land deal gave the district somewhere to hold its lessons.

place.name: Layman Road verge opposite the old Wonnerup school

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a tiny weatherboard school beside a little teacher's cottage and an apple, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Cottages On The Move
body: Not every old building at Wonnerup grew old here. The State heritage entry records a warden's cottage and tea rooms being transferred to the property in 1972. Abergeldie Cottage, built in 1922, arrived in 1984. The listing treats these introduced buildings separately from the original farm complex, recognising that they have histories of their own even though they were brought here much later.

place.name: Layman Road verge at Wonnerup House frontage

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a little weatherboard cottage riding on a friendly flatbed truck, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Missing River
body: The Wonnerup Estuary once received water from the Capel River as well as the Ludlow. In the 1860s, the Capel was diverted straight into Geographe Bay through Higgins Cut. The Ludlow still enters the estuary, although its course was also redirected. An earth bund helped form Swan Lake beside it.

place.name: Layman Road public verge near the estuary crossings

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a little river branching around a grassy island towards a blue bay, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Retired Duck Hide
body: The Wonnerup Estuary has a wooden shelter with a different history from today's bird hides. DBCA describes a substantial duck-shooting blind, probably dating from before 1930. That year, duck hunting was banned on the waters of the Wonnerup Estuary, Vasse Estuary and Vasse River. The old shelter survived the change.

place.name: Layman Road public verge overlooking the wetland system

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a duck peeking through the window of a little wooden hide, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Wartime Wetlands
body: A nature reserve between Layman Road and the Vasse Estuary contains a World War Two practice-bombing target, according to DBCA's 2019 draft wetlands plan. The document lists it among surviving historical remains, alongside old fence posts and drainage earthworks. Military training left a rather unexpected item in this wetland's heritage inventory.

place.name: Layman Road public verge near Wonnerup House

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a small vintage aeroplane above a grassy target made from concentric circles, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Deadwater, Very Much Alive
body: Despite its name, the Deadwater is a fish nursery. The City's Wonnerup coastal management plan identifies this stretch as important nursery habitat and records threatened subtropical and temperate saltmarsh around its edges. It also identifies bird nesting habitat in the surrounding dunes and riverside vegetation. A name that sounds rather lifeless belongs to a busy patch of water, mud and coastal plants.

place.name: Public shore access near Wonnerup Inlet

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of baby fish sheltering beside plump saltmarsh plants and a small nesting bird, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Otto's Long Trip
body: The blue whale skeleton called Otto at the WA Museum began its museum journey near the mouth of the Vasse River. Taxidermist Otto Lipfert oversaw three years of preparation before the 24-metre skeleton travelled by horse-drawn carriage to Busselton railway station and then by train to Perth. The whale was named after him. Years of outdoor display later left the bones noticeably whiter on one side.

place.name: Wonnerup Inlet public beach access

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a smiling blue whale skeleton resting on a tiny railway wagon, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Secondhand Classroom
body: One of Vasse's old classrooms had a life somewhere else. The Heritage Council's 2001 assessment says an old Cowaramup schoolroom was moved here in 1961 after its original school closed. It describes the building as the kind of demountable classroom used in Group Settlement areas. Alongside Vasse's own early schoolroom, it brought another community's school history into the same little schoolyard.

place.name: Kaloorup Road footpath outside the old school precinct

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a cream weatherboard classroom being carried by a little truck with an apple beside it, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Classroom That Stayed
body: Vasse's Heritage Room nearly disappeared when the school gained a new junior block in 1981. The school's own history says the Education Department wanted the old room demolished, but the community stepped in and saved and renovated it. That rescue preserved an early weatherboard classroom within a growing campus, rather than leaving its story only in photographs and former pupils' memories.

place.name: Kaloorup Road footpath at Vasse Primary School

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of friendly hands sheltering a little red weatherboard classroom, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Sailors' Schoolteachers
body: Early schooling in the Vasse district had some unusual relief teachers. The school's history says Elijah Dawson taught at his Westbrook property from 1845, but his duties as a police constable often took him away. In the 1850s and 1860s, American sailors' wives staying ashore helped with the teaching. The school traces its public-school status to 1869, well before today's campus grew around it.

place.name: Kaloorup Road public footpath beside the school

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a woman holding an open blank book beside a little sailing ship and an apple, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: A Hall That Grew
body: Vasse Hall started life in 1898 and was modified and extended in 1936, putting its expansion 38 years after the original building. The Vasse community directory lists Vasse Markets among its regular users. It also points visitors to the hall window on Kaloorup Road for the activities and services using the building, a very local noticeboard for a long-serving hall.

place.name: Kaloorup Road public frontage outside Vasse Hall

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a small community hall with a market basket and a blank noticeboard, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Two Roads, Four Names
body: When Bussell Highway was realigned around Vasse, the road names needed a workout. The City's renaming consultation covered about two kilometres of the old highway and 1.5 kilometres of Vasse-Yallingup Siding Road. Because the layout split roads into separate sections, four new names were needed for those two roads. The highway's move also changed how the smaller streets joined up.

place.name: Public footpath near Kaloorup Road and Napoleon Promenade

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of two winding roads beside four blank signposts and a tiny car, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Paint Pays For School
body: In 2021 the Vasse Art Award's first prize went to Josh Windram for Everlong. His gallery explains that he names every painting after a song. The award also helps local children: Vasse Primary School lists it among the fundraisers its P&C organises to buy school resources and equipment. The same volunteers organise colour runs, sausage sizzles and cake stalls.

place.name: Kaloorup Road footpath outside Vasse Primary School

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a paintbrush and colourful landscape painting beside a school backpack, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: A Newtown From Ireland
body: Thomas Abbey arrived in the Vasse district in 1841 with his wife Mary Ann, having come from Newtown in Ireland. He worked for John Bussell before farming independently, and began building the family homestead in 1851. They called it Newtown House. The Heritage Council says convict labour may have helped with construction, although it leaves that as a possibility rather than a certainty.

place.name: Bussell Highway public verge outside Newtown House

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of an old farmhouse beside a little suitcase and a leafy clover, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Post And New Arrivals
body: Newtown House handled two rather different kinds of arrival in the 1850s. The Abbey family home operated as a post office and a lying-in house for expectant mothers. Mary Ann Abbey was the district's midwife, and the family itself included at least five children. The City's heritage record preserves those jobs alongside the building's later life as a restaurant and function venue.

place.name: Bussell Highway public verge at Newtown House frontage

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a blank envelope beside a baby wrapped in a soft blanket outside a tiny farmhouse, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Drain With Fish
body: The Buayanyup River finishes its journey at Abbey Beach, but its last few kilometres have been straightened into a drain. Surveys in 2008 and 2009 found native fish and crayfish in the river system, including western minnows, western pygmy perch, nightfish, gilgies and marron. Freshwater shrimp and long-necked turtles were recorded too. The drainage channels are part of a much larger living waterway.

place.name: Abbey Beach public foreshore path

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a tiny minnow, a freshwater crayfish and a long-necked turtle beside reeds, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Dunes Built Back
body: Storms in May 2020 collapsed dunes west of Abbey's boat ramp. In 2024 the City rebuilt a narrow 0.4-hectare strip, using imported and local sand to make ridges and hollows. Coastal seedlings went in, with beach-access matting protecting the planting. The rebuilt dunes were intended to buffer the sea flooding inland.

place.name: Public foreshore path west of Abbey Beach boat ramp

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a rounded sand dune hugging little coastal seedlings while a blue wave curls nearby, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Sandbags Hold The Beach
body: Some of Abbey's coastal defences are bags of sand. The City describes groynes west of the boat ramp built from geotextile sand containers. For replacing a damaged timber groyne to the east, it proposed the same approach with a low profile, allowing sand to pass naturally along the shore as well.

place.name: Abbey Beach public shore path west of the boat ramp

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of plump fabric sandbags sheltering a little beach while grains drift past, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Sideways Pond
body: Broadwater's 2005 foreshore plan describes a stormwater pond at Holgate Road that overflows east along a low strip behind the front dune. It had no formal outlet into the bay. The plan says prolonged heavy rain could send water to the shore west of Norman Road, taking a sideways route first.

place.name: Public foreshore path at the northern end of Holgate Road

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a little pond sending a winding ribbon of water sideways behind a sandy dune, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Frog Trio
body: Broadwater's 2005 foreshore survey recorded moaning frogs, squelching froglets and western banjo frogs in the stormwater basin and Alan Street drain. The researchers warned that their list was incomplete: they had not surveyed at night, and the basin had recently been cleaned out. Even that limited look found three frog species.
sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of three different little frogs sitting on reeds beside a tiny banjo, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: When The Sea Visited
body: Broadwater's 2005 foreshore survey found young peppermint trees dying behind the beach. Storm surges had pushed saltwater into low areas between the dunes, killing many peppermints and some rigid wattles. The survey noted that the dead peppermints were probably recent arrivals there. Those low hollows were still within the sea's reach.
sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a surprised peppermint sapling lifting its roots above a little salty wave, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Planted Flood Buffer
body: In 2024 the City rebuilt dunes across a possible flood route west of Dolphin Road boat ramp. Work covered 0.96 hectares, using imported sand and sand shifted from nearby beaches where it was accumulating. Work in May and June took advantage of early winter rain to help the dune seedlings survive.

place.name: Public coastal path west of Dolphin Road boat ramp

sticker: A cute die-cut illustration of a row of soft sand dunes and seedlings gently holding back a blue wave, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: School Under Canvas
body: When Western Australia's first forestry school opened at Ludlow in June 1921, its buildings weren't ready. The first intake of nine apprentices was offered tents and a cook while they worked nearby. The school building followed in August, with room for 24 apprentices. Students split their training between lessons and practical work in the forests. The school closed in 1927, having trained 22 apprentices.
sticker: A cute die-cut canvas tent with a little pine sapling and an open book beside it, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Trees Packed Lunch
body: Ludlow's pine plantation began with 68,000 trees planted in 1909. By the early 1940s, its trees were supplying timber for cases and crates used to pack fresh fruit, dried fruit and processed food during the war. The first plantation thinnings had been harvested in 1936 and 1937. These pines were planted to help provide a local alternative to imported softwood and native hardwoods.
sticker: A cute die-cut wooden fruit crate with a tiny pine tree growing beside a pile of apples, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Seedlings Behind Fences
body: In June 2019, Ludlow volunteers were aiming to plant more than 100,000 tuart seedlings across 180 hectares over five years. They had help from work-release teams at Bunbury Regional Prison, who built rabbit-proof fencing around the young trees. Thirteen-year-old Bella Burgemeister joined the planting in torrential rain. The ABC report described a project that would take generations, rather than one busy planting season.
sticker: A cute die-cut tuart seedling behind a tiny protective fence while a rabbit peers through, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Flatpack Attic
body: Minninup Homestead has a possible building instruction hidden in its attic. Roman numerals cut into the floor joists may mean the timbers were fitted together on the ground before being lifted into place, according to its heritage assessment. The limestone walls used stone quarried and dressed just 100 metres away. The property was surveyed for James Kay Child in 1843, while he was also trying whaling and beer brewing.
sticker: A cute die-cut limestone farmhouse with its little attic timbers floating neatly above the roof, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Layer Cake Kilns
body: The old lime kilns near Ludlow Road North were loaded a bit like a layer cake, with timber and limestone stacked alternately for burning. The stone came from excavations close beside the kilns. Workers bagged the lime on site for building work, whitewashing houses and treating acidic farmland. The Shire's heritage record says farmers were still using the kilns in the 1920s.
sticker: A cute die-cut round stone kiln with alternating layers of pale rocks and little logs visible inside, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Runaway Wheelbarrow
body: When Higgins Cut opened through the dunes in May 1865, the rush of water carried Charles Higgins' wheelbarrow away. His diary recorded that small casualty of an ambitious attempt to drain the Capel River floodplain for farming. The channel was dug with manual labour and wheelbarrows, but it only partly worked. At high tides and during storms, seawater came back through and spread salt water over the land.
sticker: A cute die-cut wheelbarrow bobbing down a little blue channel between sandy dunes, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Rowing To School
body: In the early 1870s, Anne Higgins started a school at Springfield, the coastal farm behind Forrest Beach. Her young cousins sometimes had to row across flooded fields to reach their lessons. The Capel River's water spread behind the dunes into lakes and muddy flats, and winter travel between properties could mean taking a rowboat. Locals called this watery stretch of country the Lakes.
sticker: A cute die-cut little rowboat carrying a school satchel across a flooded paddock, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Ridges Under The Water
body: There are ridges of sand beneath the water along the southern part of Forrest Beach, extending offshore near Wonnerup Inlet. Surf Life Saving Australia's coastal description follows them north as they narrow and move closer to the beach. By Peppermint Grove Beach they have disappeared, and the shore has deeper water close in and scalloped beach cusps. The whole Forrest-Peppermint Grove beach system runs for about 14 kilometres.
sticker: A cute die-cut slice of turquoise sea showing little sandy ridges beneath a tiny floating gull, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Tiles In The Sand
body: Iluka's proposed Tutunup mine is chasing minerals that can end up in ceramic tiles and pigments. The company is targeting a chloride-ilmenite deposit for titanium dioxide and zircon. It referred the project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority in December 2021, followed by a Commonwealth referral in April 2022. The proposal would join Iluka's existing mineral-sands operations around Capel.
sticker: A cute die-cut heap of sand beside a paint pot and a small glazed tile, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: A Little Catalonia
body: Miguel Torrent arrived from Catalonia in 1905 and settled at Yoongarillup, where a small Spanish community was taking root. His wife Aurora followed in 1907 with their son Andrew. Their WA Museum Welcome Walls record lists farming and grape growing as their work in Australia. It also records a reserve and a plaque honouring the Spanish settlers, with their names gathered together on it.
sticker: A cute die-cut travelling trunk with a bunch of grapes and a small leafy vine curling around it, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: One Room, Several Jobs
body: Jindong's school served the Lennoxville Group 52 settlers and was already recorded by 1925. It followed a Public Works Department design with just one classroom and a partly enclosed verandah. The building later became a community hall used by local groups, including the Kaloorup Fire Brigade. The City now lists it as Kaloorup Hall, but its address is 335 Payne Road, Jindong.
sticker: A cute die-cut little weatherboard classroom with a school satchel and a firefighter's helmet by the door, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Orchids On The Walk
body: Gladys Anderson remembered the walk home from Jindong school as a lesson in wildflowers. Reverend Ernest Bryant visited the school monthly and sometimes walked with the children, showing them orchids and teaching their names. In her account, many Group Settlement families had come from British towns and knew little of the bush. She also recalled railway drivers and guards stopping trains to gather flowers for Bryant's wildflower shows.
sticker: A cute die-cut school satchel beside two flowering orchids and a little walking boot, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: House Goes To School
body: The teacher's house at North Jindong State School got a second life as a classroom, after leaving the district altogether. Busselton Museum dates the move to September 1983, when contractor Ashley Rains transported the house to the museum grounds in one piece. The Historical Society then paid to restore it and fit it out as a country one-room school. It began as the teacher's home, rather than the original classroom.
sticker: A cute die-cut little wooden house riding on a moving truck with a school satchel beside it, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: A Dance Built A Hall
body: Carbunup's hall began with people dancing somewhere else. A fundraising dance at Newtown Hall in 1929 helped pay for the new building, and by mid-1930 the local Parents and Citizens Association could call for construction tenders. The heritage record says it was probably built soon afterwards. The weatherboard hall hosted popular dances through the middle of the century and transferred to Yallingup Steiner School in 2016.
sticker: A cute die-cut pair of dancing shoes beside a tiny weatherboard hall, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Nearly The Same Name
body: Carbunup River acquired its extra word in 1958 because Carbunup was too easily confused with Carbarup, near Mount Barker. The townsite had been named Carbunup in 1926, taking its name from the river. That waterway had already had an English name change of its own. Captain John Molloy named it the Lennox River in 1835, in honour of Lennox Bussell.
sticker: A cute die-cut pair of blank signposts looking puzzled beside a winding blue stream, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Spiders In The Drain
body: On a September 2020 field trip, WA Naturalists' Club members found Dunsborough donkey orchids growing in a roadside spoon drain at Carbunup Reserve. A little farther along the same drain was a Carbunup king spider orchid, Caladenia procera, named for this area. Inside the reserve they found more orchids, including rusty spider orchids and rattle beaks. Their report records spring flowers beside the highway as well as inside the reserve.
sticker: A cute die-cut pink spider orchid and yellow donkey orchid peeking over the edge of a shallow grassy drain, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Coffee By The Can
body: Val Hollands remembered Acton Park Hall's monthly dances as much for the coffee as the dancing. In her recorded oral history, she described skim milk heated in a cream can sitting inside a copper, then flavoured with Robur coffee essence. People brought plates of supper, and children slept in a back room or under a cover in the ute. The teapot was much less popular than the big jug of coffee.
sticker: A cute die-cut cream can pouring coffee into a little cup beside a pair of dancing shoes, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Inland Beach
body: Yoganup gives its name to a geological formation made from an ancient shoreline. The Department of Water's geology bulletin identifies an open-cut mine near Yoganup as its reference section, where geologists describe the formation. Its layers include deposits from dunes, beaches and river deltas, with quartz sand, clay and concentrations of heavy minerals. The bulletin assigns it to the Pliocene, millions of years before the present coastline.
sticker: A cute die-cut grassy hill sliced open to reveal a tiny sandy beach and seashell beneath it, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: A River Takes A Detour
body: The upper Sabina River was given a different route in the 1920s to help keep Busselton from flooding. Its water enters the Sabina Diversion Drain, joins the Vasse Diversion Drain and reaches Geographe Bay without passing through the Vasse-Wonnerup wetlands. DWER says the diversion receives water from about 60 per cent of the Sabina catchment. The river's headwaters are up in the Whicher Range.
sticker: A cute die-cut blue stream following a bend around a tiny cluster of houses towards the sea, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Railway Plant Library
body: A botanical survey along the Ruabon-Tutunup Rail Reserve in 2005 recorded 473 plant species. Of those, 389 were local natives and 84 were introduced weeds. The reserve's 2007 management plan describes a strip about 16 kilometres long and just under 80 hectares in area, preserving vegetation communities heavily cleared elsewhere. The botanists treated their count as a working list, with room for more discoveries.
sticker: A cute die-cut short stretch of old railway track surrounded by a colourful crowd of tiny native flowers, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Cows For Science
body: In 2012, Scott and Michelle Weldon took over the Vasse Research Dairy as a commercial farm that would still be available for research. The ABC described the arrangement as a first for dairying in WA. The couple bought the existing 160-cow milking herd and brought another 200 cows from their Dardanup property. They wanted to learn from the researchers while running the dairy themselves.
sticker: A cute die-cut dairy cow looking curiously at a little magnifying glass and milk pail, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Capel's Long Shot
body: Two months before winning the 1999 Melbourne Cup, Rogan Josh had been rated a 200-to-one chance. The seven-year-old horse's breeder was based in Capel, and he only joined Bart Cummings' stable that August. He had already won the Bunbury and Pinjarra Cups with WA trainer Colin Webster. When he won on 2 November, the ABC reported hats and race books flying at Bunbury's racecourse.
sticker: A cute die-cut brown racehorse holding a golden trophy while a little hat floats in the air, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: The Flatpack Ship
body: George Payne built a 50-ton boat with help from his children, then took it apart to get it to the water. Finished in 1878 at his Capel property, it was reassembled at Fatfield and launched as the Citizen of London. The vessel was registered to trade to Geraldton with Arthur Payne as captain. Payne had hoped shipping would provide another income beyond his struggling flour mill.
sticker: A cute die-cut little wooden sailing ship with a few hull pieces fitting together like a jigsaw, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Stairway To Sea Watch
body: The big dune at Peppermint Grove Beach once had a military job. During World War II, the Australian Army put a lookout tower on top to watch for Japanese warships. The Shire describes the spot as the highest point between Bunbury and Busselton. Today's public lookout is reached by roughly 120 steps, giving walkers a very different reason to keep an eye on the bay.
sticker: A cute die-cut little lookout tower on a sandy dune with binoculars resting on its railing, with no text, letters or numbers.

title: Ten Kids, Two Rooms
body: Rushleigh began as a two-room limestone cottage built for Eugene Locke, son of John Bavage Locke of Lockville, around his marriage to Eveline Maria Reynolds in 1881. The couple raised ten children here before moving to the wheatbelt in 1910. Owners in the 1970s covered the old walls inside and out and added a big extension, so the chimneys are now the easiest part of the original cottage to spot. It's a private home, so wave from the street.

place.name: Old Timber Court, near Rushleigh

sticker: A tiny two-room stone cottage with two chimneys, bursting with ten little faces peeking out of every window

title: Named for a Farmhouse
body: Reinscourt takes its name from a Bussell family homestead that stood near where the Bussell and Vasse highways now meet. The City's heritage record says it was built by Vernon Bussell, started out as part of the original Cattle Chosen land, and was one of the district's earliest homesteads. The name was on a survey plan by 1893, but it only became a suburb on 17 December 1998, taking over the southern part of East Busselton and a slice of Wonnerup. The house itself is long gone.

place.name: Estuary Waters Drive, near the Reinscourt homestead site

sticker: A little old farmhouse with a road sign growing out of its chimney like a flower

title: One Farm, 150 Years
body: Inlet Park, home of Chapman's round stone windmill, stayed in one extended family for more than 150 years. Henry Chapman developed the farm and lived here until he died in 1859. In 1886 it passed to William Curtis, a nephew of Amelia Chapman, and the Curtis family worked the land until 20 March 1995. Since then it has been subdivided, and new streets have grown up around the 1850s brick farmhouse and the mill tower, whose machinery was made from hewn tuart timber.

place.name: Tall Tree Crescent, beside Inlet Park

sticker: A round stone windmill tower holding hands with a little brick farmhouse, both wearing birthday party hats

title: Seeds in the Post
body: The Anglican school here opened on 4 February 2003 with 128 students and is named after Georgiana Molloy. In 1836 Captain James Mangles wrote from England asking her for seeds of the local plants. For about five years she sent seeds with written descriptions and albums of pressed flowers, admired for their freshness and careful packing, and some of her albums are still at Kew. She died at Fair Lawn, her Vasse River home, on 8 April 1843, aged 37.

place.name: Hawker Approach, beside Georgiana Molloy Anglican School

sticker: A little parcel tied with string, bursting open with seeds and pressed wildflowers

title: Room for the Big Jets
body: The runway here was lengthened, widened and strengthened to 2,520 metres long and 45 metres wide, enough for wide-body jets such as the Airbus A330. The upgrade cost about $68 million and was finished in 2019. Now there are direct flights to Melbourne and Sydney, around 192,000 passengers came through in 2024 to 2025, and the airport also has a Royal Flying Doctor base. Each summer it hosts large air tankers and Helitak helicopters for fighting bushfires.

place.name: Neville Hyder Drive, Busselton Margaret River Airport

sticker: A smiling jumbo jet and a little red water-bomber helicopter sharing one long runway

title: Spuds for Mauritius
body: In November 1920 the Yalyalup Progress Association sent a deputation to Busselton asking for a guaranteed minimum price for potatoes, like the one wheat growers had. Growers including W. R. Reilly and E. Torrent brought figures on what a crop cost, and one estimate put growing and marketing at about £35 an acre, while the best Eastern States quote was just £7 10s a ton. Cables had even gone to South Africa and Mauritius to test the markets there.

place.name: Reilly Road

sticker: A cheerful potato in a sun hat sitting on a suitcase covered in travel stickers

title: Old Beaches Under the Cows
body: In 1989 the EPA cleared Cable Sands (WA) to mine what it called the Busselton Deposit, about five kilometres east of town near where the Vasse and Bussell highways meet. Under old farm pasture lay four strandlines, the lines of ancient beaches, holding about 450,000 tonnes of heavy minerals such as ilmenite, rutile and zircon. Mining was planned from 1990 to late 1993, with the topsoil saved and pasture sown again close behind the diggers so the cows could come back.

place.name: Cable Sands Road

sticker: A cow standing on a layer cake of sand stripes with shiny black mineral grains sparkling inside

title: Three Ways to Spell It
body: Landgate's place-name database lists two homesteads at exactly the same spot here: Julijoogalup and Yulijoogalup. Both first appeared on a 1973 Busselton to Augusta tourist map, and Yulijoogalup was formally approved by the Acting Surveyor General on 9 February 1982. The nearby road off Bussell Highway is spelled a third way, Uligugalup Road. Just along from it, Landgate also records a farm called Bunyip Pool, approved in December 1990.

place.name: Uligugalup Road

sticker: Three wobbly road signs pointing the same way, with a shy bunyip peeking out of a pond behind them

title: It Used to Be Fairlawn
body: Until 2000 this locality was called Fairlawn. The Council asked for a new name to avoid confusion with the historic Fairlawn property and two businesses named after it, and Bovell was approved on 24 January 2000. It honours Sir Stewart Bovell, born in Busselton in 1906, whose grandparents had arrived in the 1850s. He was the local MP from 1947 to 1971 and Minister for Lands, Forests and Immigration, then sailed for London on the Arcadia in March 1971 as Agent General.

place.name: Sir Stewart Bovell Sporting Complex, main oval

sticker: A cheerful old gentleman in a bowler hat waving from the deck of an ocean liner

title: Turf Without Grants
body: The hockey stadium at the Sir Stewart Bovell Sporting Complex got a new synthetic turf in 2019 after the old one had lasted 12 years. It cost about $250,000, and the Busselton Hockey Stadium Club raised the lot through its own fundraising with no government grants. The Busselton Hockey Association had about 1,000 players at the time, and teams from England, the Netherlands, Japan and Thailand have played on this pitch.

place.name: Busselton Hockey Stadium, Sir Stewart Bovell Sporting Complex

sticker: A hockey stick and ball sitting on a fresh green square of turf with a fat piggy bank beside them

title: Named After a Salon
body: Little Holland House, on the banks of the Vasse River, was built around 1909 to 1911 as a retirement home for Harry Prinsep and his wife Charlotte, a daughter of the pioneer John Bussell. It is named after a house in Kensington, London, where Harry spent his late teens while his aunt ran an artistic and literary salon. The painter G. F. Watts lived there and gave Harry art lessons, and Alfred Tennyson was a family friend. The Busselton house has ground-floor walls about half a metre thick.

place.name: Farmhouse Court, near Little Holland House

sticker: A half-timbered two-storey house wearing a painter's beret, with a paintbrush tucked behind its chimney

title: The Road to Augusta
body: The City's heritage list includes a stretch of No. 1 Government Road running from Strelly Street to Chapman Hill Road. It was part of a track of about 100 kilometres between the Vasse and Augusta, where the Bussells first settled. The record credits pioneer John Bussell with opening the track from 1832, and says it was the traffic route between the two settlements for about 30 years. In 1988 it was given the status of a heritage trail.

place.name: Chapman Hill Road

sticker: A dusty bush track winding between gum trees with a tiny packhorse plodding along it

title: The Missing Plaque
body: Landgate says Ambergate is possibly named after a village in Derbyshire, England, where the River Amber joins the River Derwent, and the name first turned up here on a survey plan for a school site. The weatherboard hall on Queen Elizabeth Avenue probably went up around 1925 as a school for the children of the Group 44 settlers, and it has hosted functions since 1935. A concrete plinth by the entrance once held a plaque to the first settlers, but the plaque has gone missing.

place.name: Queen Elizabeth Avenue, outside Ambergate Hall

sticker: A little weatherboard hall with a puzzled face looking at an empty plinth beside its door

title: Tents Before Farms
body: In the 1920s this patch of bush was home to Group 44 of the Group Settlement Scheme, a government plan to build a dairy industry in the South West. The settlers lived here in tents before being given nearby land to clear for farming. Families came from other parts of Australia and from Britain, with land and subsidies for stock, but many blocks never paid their way. After two Royal Commissions the scheme was abandoned in the early 1930s.

place.name: Ambergate Reserve Loop, north side

sticker: A small canvas tent in the bush with a milk can and an axe leaning against it

title: Boots in the Bath
body: Ambergate Reserve is 75 hectares of the shrubland and woodland that once covered much of the southern Swan Coastal Plain. Mapping shows three threatened ecological communities cover more than 80 per cent of it, and it shelters quenda and a rare Verticordia, or feather flower. Jarrah dieback is a serious threat, so walkers are asked to step through the foot bath at the information shelter before setting off. The Busselton Naturalists Club managed the reserve from 1987 to 2021.

place.name: Ambergate Reserve Loop, north-east side

sticker: A quenda splashing happily in a little tub of footbath water next to a pair of hiking boots

title: The Storekeepers' Name
body: Kealy was proposed as a locality by the Shire of Busselton in June 1987 and approved that November. Landgate's record says it is believed to honour an early settler, and possibly Terence Joseph Kealy, who lived from 1877 to 1953, and his son Gerald Patrick Kealy. Both were storekeepers at Vasse and owned farm lots in Broadwater. The record keeps that possibly, so treat it as the likely story rather than a settled fact.

place.name: Locke Nature Reserve

sticker: An old-fashioned shop counter with a brass bell, a set of scales and a paper bag of sweets

title: The Tall Mast
body: The masts beside Caves Road belong to the ABC's radio transmitter, which the City's heritage list calls a local landmark. A 1987 staff newsletter says station 6BS was commissioned on 22 December 1969, broadcasting on 680 kHz from a 46 metre tower. A 183 metre mast took over on 27 May 1971, and in 1979 the frequency moved to 684 kHz. The newsletter said its signal reached south to Cape Leeuwin, inland to Collie and up the coast towards Perth.

place.name: Caves Road verge, outside the ABC transmitter

sticker: A very tall skinny radio mast wearing headphones, with little musical notes floating off the top

title: A Rope Bridge for Possums
body: In July 2013 a 26.5 metre rope bridge was strung across Caves Road here, linking peppermint trees in Locke Nature Reserve with trees on the far side. It was built for the endangered western ringtail possum. Possums were inspecting the poles within a week, and over 270 nights of monitoring the cameras logged about 1,300 complete crossings, including mothers carrying young. No other mammals were recorded using it, though a few birds stopped for a rest.

place.name: Locke Nature Reserve, south end of the Caves Road possum bridge

sticker: A ringtail possum with a baby on its back tightrope-walking across a rope bridge over a road

title: Named for a Lost Launch
body: Siesta Park is named after a boat. The resort's own history says Ivan and Dulcie Tickle bought this beachfront property soon after the war, in 1946, and named it after Ivan's launch, the Siesta. The launch had served in the Naval Auxiliary Patrol and, as the family tells it, caught fire and was lost during a rescue for a downed aircraft over Cockburn Sound. The compensation largely paid for the land. Landgate's record simply says the Tickles sailed the Siesta on the Swan River.

place.name: Siesta Park Road

sticker: A little wooden motor launch having a snooze on the water, with a nightcap and a trail of Z bubbles

title: The Holy Mile
body: This stretch of coast is the Locke Estate, 37.5 hectares of Crown land that the City of Busselton runs as 16 campsites. Every one is leased to a not-for-profit group, from the Scouts and Legacy to Adventist, Baptist, Catholic, Anglican and Uniting church groups. All that church camping explains the local nickname, and the Uniting Church's brochure says its camp sits on the Holy Mile. The current leases run until 2032.

place.name: Dunsborough to Busselton Shared Path, beside the Locke Estate

sticker: A row of little camping tents along a beach, each with a tiny steeple or flag on top

title: A Title Twice as Big
body: When Location 5 was granted to Richard Gale in 1892, its title ran to the high water mark. The resort's own history says that original block was about twice the size of the property today, which shows how much land the sea has taken. In 1915 Angus Gilchrist built six simple cottages here and called it Peppermint Park. In 2025 the City put out a draft plan for eight rock groynes along the coast just west of here to hold the sand in place.

place.name: Siesta Park Road, north bend

sticker: A wave taking a cheeky bite out of a sandy beach shaped like a slice of toast

title: Molloy's Ditch
body: In the 1850s sandbanks stopped the Lennox River from reaching the sea, and in winter its water spread across the low ground. Captain John Molloy had a channel cut between the river and the shore, and it became known as Molloy's Ditch. The fight with the water carried on: from 1928 a weir with floodgates was built upstream, and its jarrah stop boards were later swapped for Oregon ones because the jarrah was too heavy to lift.

place.name: Smith Street, near Molloy's Ditch

sticker: A stern little man in a top hat holding a shovel next to a river squeezing through a narrow sandy channel

title: The Grave That Moved
body: Off Chain Avenue stand the roofless limestone walls of the old Marybrook farmhouse. Captain John Molloy first held this land, then local farmer Richard Gale. Molloy's grandson Edward Richardson-Bunbury bought the lot in 1889 and built the stone house, later farming draught horses and dairy cattle there with his wife Vida. When Edward died he was buried in the churchyard next door, but when that church closed, both his body and the church building were moved to Dunsborough.

place.name: Chain Avenue, near the Marybrook farmhouse

sticker: A tiny wooden church riding on the back of a truck, waving goodbye to a stone farmhouse

title: Named by the Railway
body: Marybrook started out as a railway siding. Its name was approved on 5 October 1923 for a stop on the Busselton to Flinders Bay line, out between the Mary Brook drain and the Carbunup River. When the line closed, the name stayed on as the name of the district, and it was made an official bounded locality on 13 November 1987. The area also takes in Group Settlement number 144, which was known as Marybrook too.

place.name: Marybrook Road, near the old siding

sticker: A little steam train stopped beside a tiny platform with a babbling brook running under it
